text: I bought a new phone yesterday.
why: The sentence has no mistake at all; 'a new phone' is correct.

text: I want to ___ a new job next year.
why: 'take a new job' (accept a job) is also correct.

text: I need to ___ an appointment with the doctor.
why: 'get an appointment with the doctor' is also standard, especially in British English.

text: She ___ the bus to work every day.
why: 'rides the bus to work' is standard American English.

text: I want to ___ my English this year. (BETTER)
why: 'improve' is not a form of BETTER; 'better' is itself a verb ('to better my English'), so the answer is missing it. A different word is a poor fit for a formation item.

text: My brother plays football on Sundays.
why: The alternative 'on Sunday' is a different word that sounds different; it should not be accepted as the same sentence.

text: My brother and sister is students.
why: The fourth part is an empty string; it needs 4 real parts.

text: Please ___ on the lights; it is dark.
why: 'put on the lights' is correct British English.

text: I want to ___ a reservation for two people.
why: 'get a reservation' is also natural, especially in American English.

text: I usually ___ up at seven o’clock.
why: 'get up at seven o'clock' is equally correct.

text: If it ___ tomorrow, we will stay at home.
why: 'If it is raining tomorrow, ...' is also grammatical and natural.

text: She said she ___ call me later.
why: 'She said she will call me later' is acceptable when the call is still in the future; backshift is optional.

text: He asked me where I ___.
why: 'where I work' is acceptable if it is still true; backshift is optional, so the explanation is too absolute.

text: She decided to ___ up smoking last year.
why: 'take up smoking' is also correct (opposite meaning, but grammatical and natural).

text: The meeting was ___ off because of the storm.
why: 'put off' (postponed) is also correct.

text: He wants to ___ for a new position at work.
why: 'ask for a new position at work' is also correct English.

text: She is used to wake up early.
why: Two possible fixes: 'is used to waking up' or 'She used to wake up', so 'is used to' is also a valid answer.

text: We need to ___ down the main ideas before writing.
why: 'write down', 'put down' and 'take down' are all correct.

text: This decision was completely ___. (REASON)
why: 'reasonable' also fits ('completely reasonable'); the answer must list it or the sentence needs negative context.

text: The manager insisted that every order ___ checked twice.
why: British English often uses the indicative after insist ('is/was checked'); British/American difference decides the answer.

text: I would rather you ___ the report today.
why: 'I would rather you finish' (subjunctive) is acceptable, especially in American English.

text: The contract is ___ to change without written agreement.
why: 'not likely' is also correct ('is not likely to change'); the 'unlikely to' option gives 'to to'; the explanation says 'to' follows, which confuses the options.

text: The number of customers have increased this year.
why: The fourth part is an empty string; it needs 4 real parts.

text: She suggested that he goes to the doctor.
why: 'suggested that he goes' is accepted in informal British English; British/American difference decides the answer.

text: I am looking forward to hear from you.
why: This is a B1 point, already tested in the B1 files; too easy for B2.

text: We need to ___ up with a solution before Friday.
why: 'come up with' is B1 and already in the B1 files; too easy for B2.

text: He was ___ up by the difficult questions.
why: 'thrown up' means 'vomited'; the idiom is 'thrown (off) by'. The answer and explanation are wrong.
